reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Suspect it in a neonate or infant with unexplained high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and haemolytic anaemia
Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GSS, encoding glutathione synthetase
The biochemical hallmark is 5-oxoprolinuria (pyroglutamic aciduria) with elevated 5-oxoproline in blood and urine
Severity is a spectrum: a mild form limited to haemolytic anaemia, a moderate form with acidosis and haemolysis, and a severe form adding progressive neurological impairment
Neurological features in severe disease include developmental delay, seizures, ataxia and, over time, spasticity
Management focuses on correcting acidosis, supporting antioxidant defences (for example with vitamins C and E) and avoiding oxidative and other stressors
Glutathione depletion leaves red cells and neurones vulnerable to oxidative damage
5-oxoproline can also accumulate from acquired causes (such as certain drugs), so genetic and enzymatic confirmation matters
reference.pathophysiology: Glutathione synthetase catalyses the second step of glutathione synthesis, joining gamma-glutamylcysteine with glycine. In its deficiency, glutathione is not formed, removing feedback inhibition on the first enzyme of the gamma-glutamyl cycle; gamma-glutamylcysteine is instead diverted to 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamate), which accumulates and causes a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and 5-oxoprolinuria. The lack of glutathione, the cell's principal antioxidant, leaves erythrocytes prone to oxidative haemolysis and, in severe disease, allows oxidative injury to the central nervous system with progressive neurological impairment. Treatment supports acid-base balance and antioxidant defences while limiting oxidative stress.
additionalDifferentials: Other organic acidaemias causing high anion-gap acidosis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and other haemolytic anaemias
Sepsis or inborn errors presenting with neonatal acidosis
additionalInvestigations: GSS molecular genetic testing and/or erythrocyte glutathione synthetase enzyme assay
Blood gas and anion-gap assessment for metabolic acidosis
Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film for haemolysis
Neuroimaging in patients with neurological features
redFlags: Severe or decompensated metabolic acidosis in a neonate
Deterioration during oxidative stress, infection or exposure to oxidant drugs
reference.prognosis: Mild disease may be limited to compensated haemolysis with a good outlook, whereas the severe form carries a risk of progressive neurological impairment; early correction of acidosis and antioxidant support improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing 5-oxoprolinuria solely to acquired drug causes and missing the inherited defect
Overlooking haemolytic anaemia as a clue to the underlying enzyme deficiency
Failing to protect patients from oxidative stressors and oxidant drugs
Confusing it with 5-oxoprolinase deficiency, which has a different mechanism and course
references: OMIM entry for Glutathione Synthetase Deficiency (GSS)
Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Correct the high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with alkali therapy such as sodium bicarbonate or citrate
Support antioxidant defences with vitamin C and vitamin E supplementation to compensate for the glutathione deficit
Advise avoidance of oxidative and other stressors, including oxidant drugs, that provoke haemolysis
Manage the haemolytic anaemia supportively, with red-cell transfusion for severe episodes and folic acid supplementation
In severe disease treat seizures with antiseizure medication and provide neurorehabilitation and developmental support
Monitor acid-base status, the full blood count, haemolytic markers and neurological progress over time
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive GSS inheritance, including recurrence risk and family testing
